title: Thermomix TM7 After Three Months: Is a $1,600 Blender Worth It?
creator: Hannah Vogel
description:
I bought a Thermomix TM7 in June with my own money after years of saying I never would. Here's what three months of daily use actually looks like.

What I cooked in this video: risotto, bread dough, hollandaise.

0:50 How you even buy one
1:50 Risotto test
2:50 The annoying parts
3:50 Verdict

sentences.t: For about five years I have made fun of people who own a Thermomix.
My sister has one, my neighbor has one, and every time they talked about it, it sounded like a cult.
And then in June, I bought a Thermomix TM7, so, here we are, I'm in the cult now.
This is three months of using it pretty much every day, and I'll be honest about the parts I don't love.
First, the weird part, which is how you actually get one of these.
You can't walk into a store and buy a Thermomix, at least not here in Germany.
Thermomix is sold through consultants, so you book a cooking demo, someone comes to your house, and they cook you lunch in it.
Mine was a lovely retired teacher called Ulla, and she made a lemon curd in about seven minutes while I stood there with my mouth open.
The TM7 costs fifteen hundred and ninety nine euros, and you pay it through the consultant, or in monthly installments if you want.
It comes with a free trial of Cookidoo, which is the Thermomix recipe platform, and after that it's a yearly subscription.
And I know, I know, that whole setup sounds like a pyramid scheme, and I'm not going to pretend it doesn't feel a bit like one.
Okay, so, what is it actually?
It's a blender, a scale, a stove, a steamer and a mixer, all in one jug with a heating element underneath.
The new screen is huge, and it walks you through recipes step by step, it weighs as you pour, it sets the heat and the time.
Let's do the test I always do, which is risotto, because risotto punishes you for walking away.
Onion and garlic in, chop for five seconds, then sauté with butter for three minutes.
Rice in, a splash of white wine, then stock, and then I just close the lid and leave.
The blade runs in reverse on a slow setting, so it stirs instead of chopping.
Eighteen minutes later, and look at that, it's creamy, it's not mush, the rice still has a bit of bite.
Is it as good as when I stand there stirring for half an hour with a glass of wine?
Ninety percent as good, and I got to fold laundry instead, so honestly I'll take it.
Now, the annoying stuff, because there is plenty.
The jug only holds about two liters, so for a family of five I'm cooking pasta sauce in two batches.
Browning meat is basically impossible, it steams instead of searing, so I still use a pan for that.
A lot of the best recipes are locked behind that subscription, and I hate paying yearly for recipes.
And when it's kneading bread dough it walks across the counter like it's trying to escape.
The hollandaise, though, I have to show you the hollandaise, because this is where it earns its money.
It holds the sauce at exactly the right temperature while it whisks, and it has never split on me, not once.
I have split hollandaise by hand more times than I want to admit on the internet.
So, is it worth it?
If you cook every single day and you hate standing at the stove, probably yes, it's paid for itself in takeaway I didn't order.
If you love the actual act of cooking, or you mostly cook big batches, I'd honestly save your money.
I'm keeping mine, I'm a little embarrassed about it, and my sister will never let me forget this.
Tell me in the comments if you've got one sitting in a cupboard gathering dust, I want to know.
